path.title: Polars DataFrames
path.summary: Expressions, lazy queries and joins with real Polars, run as trusted local Python only when you enable it.

lessons.title: Expressions: columns in, columns out
lessons.summary: Build transformations from pl.col expressions inside select, with_columns, filter and group_by().agg, and handle nulls on purpose.

blocks.title: An expression describes a column
blocks.body: pl.col("amount") * 1.2 is not a value: it is a recipe that Polars evaluates inside a context. select keeps only the expressions you list; with_columns adds or replaces columns; filter keeps the rows where a boolean expression is true; group_by(...).agg(...) evaluates expressions per group. The expressions of one context run in parallel and cannot see each other's new columns: chain another with_columns for that.

blocks.title: Conditions and nulls
blocks.body: pl.when(condition).then(a).otherwise(b) is the CASE WHEN of Polars. A comparison with null gives null, and filter treats null as false. is_null(), fill_null() and eq_missing() make the choice explicit. count() counts non-null values; pl.len() counts rows.

blocks.title: No Python loops over rows
blocks.body: map_elements with a Python lambda runs row by row in Python, loses the engine's speed and hides the logic from the query plan. Look for an expression first: the str, dt and list namespaces cover most text, date and list work.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict impressions, clicks and spend per campaign. clicked_at is null when the ad was shown but not clicked.

code.source:
import polars as pl

events = pl.DataFrame({
    "campaign_id": ["spring", "spring", "spring", "summer", "summer"],
    "amount": [1.0, 2.5, None, 4.0, 1.5],
    "clicked_at": ["2026-03-01", None, "2026-03-02", None, None],
})

result = (
    events
    .with_columns(pl.col("clicked_at").str.to_date())
    .with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("amount").is_null()).then(0.0).otherwise(pl.col("amount")).alias("amount_filled")
    )
    .group_by("campaign_id")
    .agg(
        pl.len().alias("impressions"),
        pl.col("clicked_at").count().alias("clicks"),
        pl.col("amount_filled").sum().alias("spend"),
    )
    .sort("campaign_id")
)
display(result)

steps.title: Data with nulls
steps.body: Five events; one amount and three clicked_at values are null.

steps.title: Parse, then derive
steps.body: The first with_columns parses the date; the second one can use the parsed column and fills the missing amount with when/then.

steps.title: Aggregate per group
steps.body: agg evaluates three expressions for each campaign_id: one output row per campaign.

steps.title: count() versus len()
steps.body: pl.len() counts every row (impressions); count() on clicked_at skips nulls (clicks): spring 3 and 2, summer 2 and 0.

lessons.title: Lazy frames and the query plan
lessons.summary: Describe the whole query with scan_* or .lazy(), let the optimizer push filters and projections down, then collect once.

blocks.title: Eager versus lazy
blocks.body: A DataFrame runs each method as soon as you call it. A LazyFrame (pl.scan_parquet, pl.scan_csv or df.lazy()) records the steps and runs nothing until collect(). Because the optimizer sees the whole query, it reads only the columns used (projection pushdown), applies filters while reading (predicate pushdown) and skips work whose result is never used.

blocks.title: Read the plan
blocks.body: lf.explain() prints the optimized plan; read it from the bottom up: the scan first, then filters, joins and aggregations. In Datapass, display(lazy_frame) collects it and shows Polars' own plan next to the rows: the real output of LazyFrame.explain(), not a model.

blocks.title: Collect once
blocks.body: Calling collect() in the middle and continuing on the DataFrame splits the query in two: the optimizer can no longer push a later filter into the scan. Stay lazy until the end. collect() keeps the whole result in memory; sink_parquet writes a large result to disk in streaming mode instead.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the revenue per customer. Then find in the plan where the filter on status is applied and which columns are read.

code.source:
import polars as pl

orders = pl.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    "customer_id": ["A", "B", "A", "C", "B"],
    "status": ["DONE", "OPEN", "DONE", "DONE", "CANCELLED"],
    "amount": [40.0, 15.0, 60.0, 90.0, 20.0],
    "note": ["", "call back", "", "gift", ""],
}).lazy()

query = (
    orders
    .filter(pl.col("status") == "DONE")
    .group_by("customer_id")
    .agg(pl.col("amount").sum().alias("revenue"), pl.len().alias("orders"))
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
)
display(query)

steps.title: Make it lazy
steps.body: .lazy() turns the DataFrame into a LazyFrame: nothing is computed yet.

steps.title: Describe, do not run
steps.body: filter, group_by, agg and sort only add nodes to the plan.

steps.title: Collect and see the plan
steps.body: display() collects the query once and shows the optimized plan from LazyFrame.explain().

steps.title: Unused columns are dropped
steps.body: note and order_id are never used, so the optimized plan does not carry them.

lessons.title: Joins in Polars
lessons.summary: Join DataFrames with how="left", "inner", "semi", "anti" and "full", and keep a left join when you filter the right side.

blocks.title: The same row logic as SQL
blocks.body: df.join(other, on="customer_id", how="left") matches rows with equal keys and keeps unmatched left rows with nulls on the right. Duplicate keys multiply rows exactly as in SQL. how="semi" keeps the left rows that have a match, once each, and adds no column; how="anti" keeps those that have none.

blocks.title: Null keys
blocks.body: By default a null key matches nothing, as in SQL. The nulls_equal=True option (join_nulls in older Polars versions) makes null match null: use it only when a null key really identifies one thing.

blocks.title: Filter before, not after
blocks.body: Filtering the joined frame on a right-side column (status == "COMPLETED") removes the unmatched rows, whose status is null: the left join silently becomes an inner join. Filter the right frame first, then join.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the row count of each result and which customers keep a null order_id.

code.source:
import polars as pl

customers = pl.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["Ada", "Ben", "Chloe"]})
orders = pl.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "customer_id": [1, 1, 2, None],
    "status": ["COMPLETED", "OPEN", "OPEN", "COMPLETED"],
})

completed = orders.filter(pl.col("status") == "COMPLETED")
kept = customers.join(completed, on="customer_id", how="left")
lost = customers.join(orders, on="customer_id", how="left").filter(pl.col("status") == "COMPLETED")
without_orders = customers.join(orders, on="customer_id", how="anti")

display(pl.DataFrame({
    "result": ["filter then join", "join then filter", "anti join"],
    "rows": [kept.height, lost.height, without_orders.height],
}))

steps.title: Filter the right side first
steps.body: Ada keeps order 101; Ben and Chloe stay with a null order: 3 rows.

steps.title: Filtering after the join drops rows
steps.body: Ben and Chloe have a null status after the left join, so the filter removes them: 1 row.

steps.title: Anti join
steps.body: Only Chloe has no order at all. The order with a null customer_id matches nobody.

steps.title: Compare the counts
steps.body: The same data gives 3, 1 and 1 rows: the order of filter and join changes the answer.
